source.title: Universal Neurons in GPT2 Language Models
source.authors: Wes Gurnee; T. Horsley; Zifan Carl Guo; Tara Rezaei Kheirkhah; Qinyi Sun; W. Hathaway; Neel Nanda; Dimitris Bertsimas

page_placements.theme: Cross-seed and cross-model universality is linked to unit interpretability

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses polysemanticity but does not measure whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Its experiments measure cross-seed neuron universality and interpretability, different constructs from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper states that individual neurons are often polysemantic and hypothesizes that universal neurons are more likely to be monosemantic. Its own results concern activation correlations across independently seeded models and interpretations of selected universal neurons, not the frequency or causes of polysemantic responses. No claim-version labels are warranted.
record.test_reason: The paper measures cross-seed neuron universality (excess activation correlation) in GPT2 and Pythia models and interprets the selected universal neurons. It states as background that neurons are often polysemantic, and hypothesises that universal neurons are monosemantic. It never measures how many neurons respond to unrelated inputs, what causes polysemanticity, or how measurement choices change the count. Universality is a related but different construct. The skew/kurtosis contrast between universal and non-universal neurons is only suggestive of monosemanticity; it is not a polysemanticity rate.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find only about 1-5% of neurons universal across seeds and read this as evidence that individual neurons are not the right unit of analysis. The few universal neurons are often interpretable, form families, and often have near-duplicates and clear functional roles. Examples are entropy neurons, attention-deactivation neurons, and prediction/suppression neurons that often form antipodal pairs. The authors do not measure how common polysemanticity is.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares neuron activation correlations across random-seed language models and interprets selected units; it does not apply the original sources' vision-neuron analyses or test polysemantic response mixtures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported universal-neuron share differs across the tested model settings: GPT2-small is higher than GPT2-medium and Pythia-160M.

fits_no_version.finding: Only 1.23% (GPT2-medium), 1.26% (Pythia-160M) and 4.16% (GPT2-small) of neurons have excess cross-seed correlation >0.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Few individual MLP neurons are universal across random seeds in small language models.

fits_no_version.finding: Universal neurons have high pre-activation skew and kurtosis, large negative bias and sparse activation. Non-universal neurons have roughly Gaussian pre-activation statistics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-seed universal neurons show the activation statistics expected of monosemantic neurons. Whether non-universal neurons are polysemantic is not measured.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected universal neurons usually have clear interpretations and fall into families: unigram, alphabet, previous-token, position, syntax, semantic and prediction/suppression.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons selected by cross-seed activation correlation are often interpretable.

record.problems: The experiments use a narrow setting: GPT2 models trained from different random seeds, with supporting Pythia experiments. Interpretations rely in part on manual analysis and algorithmic supervision. The paper does not directly test the claim's polysemanticity outcomes.

untested.parts: No share of polysemantic MLP neurons is measured. Non-universal neurons are not tested for responses to unrelated inputs.
Superposition is not tested as a cause.
Initialization, regularization or noise are not tested as causes of polysemanticity. Seed variation is used only to measure universality.
Activation function, architecture and regularization are not varied with a polysemanticity measure.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
The dependence of polysemanticity judgments on activation range or explanation scoring is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: Section 6.2 speculates that duplicate neurons may be polysemantic over different rarer features. This is a hypothesis, not a measurement. Polysemanticity is cited only as background (Olah 2020b, SoLU, Toy Models).

versions.untested_parts: Does not test polysemantic responses in vision models or InceptionV1.
Does not measure the share of language-model neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Does not test whether capacity pressure or superposition causes polysemanticity.
Does not test polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure or its possible causes.
Although it includes multiple model families and sizes, it does not measure how architecture, activation function, or regularization changes polysemanticity or its performance cost.
Does not re-examine canonical polysemantic neurons to determine whether their mixed responses share a feature.
Does not test whether polysemanticity judgments depend on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: GPT2-medium-a
rows.operation_detail: Measured each neuron's excess correlation, comparing its maximum activation correlation across other seeded models with a random-rotated-basis baseline.

conditions.value: 100 million tokens from the Pile test set

rows.measure: Share/count of neurons above the excess-correlation threshold
rows.baseline: Random rotated-basis correlation baseline is subtracted to obtain excess correlation.
rows.value: 1253 out of 98304 neurons have excess correlation greater than 0.5; the paper later reports 1.23% for GPT2-medium.
rows.note: Measures cross-model universality, not whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1 Results: 1253 of 98304 neurons in GPT2-medium-a have excess correlation >0.5; 1.23% given later in 4.1 and 6.3

rows.operation_detail: Measured the share of neurons with excess activation correlation across seeds, relative to a random-rotated-basis baseline.

conditions.value: 100 million tokens from the Pile test set

rows.measure: Share of neurons above the excess-correlation threshold
rows.baseline: Random rotated-basis correlation baseline is subtracted to obtain excess correlation.
rows.note: The reported share concerns universality across seeds, not polysemantic responses.

rows.subject: Pythia-160m
rows.operation_detail: Measured the share of neurons with excess activation correlation across models, relative to a random-rotated-basis baseline.

conditions.value: Pythia models; five models are referenced in the weight analysis
100 million tokens from the Pile test set

rows.measure: Share of neurons above the excess-correlation threshold
rows.baseline: Random rotated-basis correlation baseline is subtracted to obtain excess correlation.
rows.note: This is a universality statistic, not a measure of mixed or unrelated neuron responses.

source_check.correct: Pythia-160m compared with models b-e (Figure 13 caption; per Section 4.1 the same cross-seed experiment repeated). The five Pythia models (410M to 6.9B) belong only to the unembedding-kurtosis weight analysis (Section 5.1, Figure 22), not to this correlation value.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1 (repeat on Pythia-160m, Figure 13); Figure 13 caption; Section 5.1 / Figure 22 for the five Pythia models
source_check.problem: Condition mixes in the five Pythia models (410M-6.9B) from the weight analysis, which are not the models compared for the 1.26% value.

rows.subject: GPT2-medium-a
rows.operation_detail: Manually inspected selected neurons with excess correlation above 0.5 and grouped them into neuron families using automated tests and qualitative analysis.

conditions.value: manual inspection and automated tests based on vocabulary and spaCy labels

rows.measure: Qualitative interpretability of selected universal neurons
rows.value: The authors report that these neurons usually have clear interpretations and can be grouped into a smaller number of neuron families.
rows.note: This concerns selected universal neurons; it does not establish how often neurons generally have one coherent job or whether purportedly mixed inputs share a feature.
rows.check: This is a qualitative interpretation of neurons selected by excess correlation >0.5, which is a selection-based subset. It gives no rate of polysemantic versus monosemantic neurons, so it cannot bear on V2 or V6.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Cites polysemanticity as well known and hypothesises universal neurons are monosemantic, but never measures how many neurons respond to unrelated inputs.

tranche.reason: Measures cross-seed neuron universality, not polysemanticity. Polysemanticity appears only as background, a hypothesis (universal neurons more likely monosemantic) and an untested speculation in 6.2.

source_check.notes: Shares an author (Gurnee) with an original source. Internal inconsistency in the paper: 1253/98304 = 1.27%, yet it reports 1.23% for GPT2-medium. The text does not say what the Pythia-160m comparison models b-e are. Universality percentages do not measure the share of polysemantic neurons.
